2026-11-23 · Metacheck 0.4.4.35

To fix (1)

To fix Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed 24 Python code files for reproducibility and ran 9 of them.
  • 13 Python files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run.
  • 7 of 9 Python scripts ran without error when executed (13 more files are imported by other files, not run on their own).
  • Of the others, 1 did not reproduce and 1 could not be checked automatically.
  • 7 installable Python dependencies detected.

Note

See the section Reproducibility Check below for the details.

To check (4)

To check Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 11 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 31 of 185 data columns (17%) are documented in a codebook; 154 are not.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 3 codebook/README/label sources and 185 data columns across 20 files.

What we found

  • The OSF project https://osf.io/ngp3k is private. Metacheck examined the files through the view_only link. As the preprint is public, and the OSF Files are accessible to anyone, consider making the OSF project public.
  • We found 3445 files in 1 repository.
  • We found 0 README files and 0 repositories without READMEs.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 8 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 185 columns across 20 data files.

Issues Identified

5 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

File Column Issues
coherence_review.csv Her message as sent 🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 62 characters, 94% distinct, 83% written i…
coherence_review.csv Misfit turn? 🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (“?”)
coherence_review.csv Questions in the AI’s previous reply 🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Free-text column (median 183 characters, 97% distinct, 23% written …
coherence_review.csv Reviewer note 🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: looks fine/Looks fine
coherence_review.csv Selection error? 🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (“?”)

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 20 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. The code reads files that are only inside registration_deposit_v1.zip, 05_code.zip, 06_analysis_v2.zip, and no script unpacks them. We unpacked them in their folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks them (such as zipfile.ZipFile("registration_deposit_v1.zip").extractall() in Python), or upload the files unpacked.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 22 scripts: 7 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 13 files were not run on their own, because other files import them: report.py (by run.py); selector.py (by runner.py, run.py); providers.py (by mock.py, runner.py, judge.py, run.py); export.py (by run.py); inputs.py (by judge.py, app.py, run.py); route.py (by run.py); mock.py (by run.py); batch.py (by run.py); runner.py (by batch.py, judge.py, run.py); judge.py (by batch.py, run.py); normalise.py (by export.py, judge.py); app.py (by run.py); resolutions.py (by build.py). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt).

Duplicate files across repo mirrors

13 files are byte-identical to another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component that mirrors the same materials). They were only run once, from its first occurrence, to avoid wasted duplicate execution: report.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/report.py (same as report.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/report.py); selector.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/selector.py (same as selector.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/selector.py); providers.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/providers.py (same as providers.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/providers.py); export.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/export.py (same as export.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/export.py); inputs.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/inputs.py (same as inputs.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/inputs.py); route.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/route.py (same as route.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/route.py); mock.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/mock.py (same as mock.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/mock.py); batch.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/batch.py (same as batch.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/batch.py); runner.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/runner.py (same as runner.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/runner.py); judge.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/judge.py (same as judge.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/judge.py); normalise.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/normalise.py (same as normalise.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/normalise.py); app.py at 05_code.zip/code/audit/app.py (same as app.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/audit/app.py); run.py at 05_code.zip/code/run.py (same as run.py at registration_deposit_v1.zip/code/run.py).

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Practical guidance is among the three most common topics in ChatGPT conversations (Chatterji et al., 2025), and in a randomised trial that included career topics, about three in four participants reported following the advice they received (Luettgau et al., 2026).

Ethics approval statement:

Before submission we asked the FAccT programme committee for guidance; they advised that ethics approval is not mandatory and that possible concerns should be addressed transparently in the paper.

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
